claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the suppression of brittle secondary-phase formation during cooling.
Maintaining a single-phase or homogeneously disordered microstructure reduces internal stress concentrations at grain boundaries.
Reduced internal stress concentrations at grain boundaries preserve toughness.
The initial as-cast alloy has a mixed microstructure.
Regions in the initial microstructure may form brittle secondary phases during slow cooling.
A sufficiently high-temperature solution treatment dissolves secondary phases.
Rapid cooling minimizes the time available for diffusion-driven phase segregation.
Minimizing diffusion-driven segregation inhibits the formation of brittle secondary phases.
A more uniform, metastable single-phase microstructure has fewer preferential crack-initiation sites at phase boundaries.
Reducing preferential crack-initiation sites at phase boundaries increases retained fracture toughness.
Rapidly cooled specimens will have a finer and more uniform microstructure than slow-cooled specimens.
Rapidly cooled specimens will have statistically higher toughness or fracture energy than slow-cooled specimens.
Slow cooling permits the growth of coarser precipitates or brittle secondary phases.
The hypothesis applies where the relevant diffusion mechanisms are active only at elevated temperatures, stated as roughly above 800–1000 °C.
The hypothesis applies where alloy composition favors formation of a disordered solid solution.
The proposed behavior may not hold when severe compositional segregation or intermetallic formation dominates microstructural evolution.
